newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Tenaga bonds seen aimed at improving grid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tenaga bonds seen aimed at improving grid.

text.p: Malaysia's Tenaga Nasional Bhd is expected to use the proceeds of an $800 million Yankee bond issue to fund improvements on its transmission and distribution network, analysts said on Friday.

The state-controlled power utility's two-tranche bond offering was priced on Thursday. It is selling $500 million of non-callable 10-year notes and $300 million of 10-year securities with a five-year put option.
Analysts said Tenaga's capital expenditure needs are five billion ringgit ($2.5 billion) a year.

The funds raised from the Yankee bond issue will go towards projects such as building more substations and upgrading Malaysia's national power grid from 275 kV to 500 kV, said analyst William Lean at HSBC James Capel.
After a series of embarrassing nationwide blackouts, including a major one last August, Tenaga has been working to upgrade its transmission and distribution capabilities.
Another analyst at a local brokerage said other upgrading projects involve replacing cables with thicker lines.
Tenaga is capable of generating about two to three billion ringgit from internal funds to make up the balance of its capital expenditure budget, he added.
An "A+" rating on Tenaga's debt from Standard & Poor's should keep demand for the paper healthy, the analyst said.
"That recognises Tenaga's ability to repay on its debt," he said. "I don't see any problem why foreign investors won't take up Tenaga's debt."
Tenaga, which generates about 70 percent of Malaysia's electricity, used the Labuan offshore financial centre for the first time as the underwriting base for the Yankee bonds.
Labuan, off the coast of Borneo island, was established as an offshore financial centre by Malaysia in 1990 in an attempt to woo funds from other tax-free havens.

Analysts said tariff increases were a key challenge for Tenaga and its financial ratings. Pressured by the high cost of buying power from independent power producers (IPPs) and large capital spending plans, Tenaga badly needs to raise tariffs.

Tenaga is rumoured to have asked the government for as much as a 20 percent increase in tariffs, analysts said. "We think they should get some tariff increase, but not to the extent that they asked for," said Janelle Chuah, an analyst at Jupiter Securities, who forecast a rate boost of five to 10 percent.
Analysts said the utility, which is about 80-percent-owned by the goverment, is also seeking subsidies for its energy costs and tax reductions.
Tenaga officials, currently on a New York roadshow for the bond issue, could not be reached for comment.
